rv.q: The everyday poison known as toxic masculinity becomes dangerously easy to swallow in “Linda Vista,” Tracy Letts’s inspired, ruthless take on the classic midlife-crisis comedy.
Tracy Letts has written a deeply personal, funny and ultimately heartbreaking play about midlife crisis and the search for meaning.
These aren’t particularly fresh characters or situations, but Dexter Bullard’s staging and the Steppenwolf cast lend them an appealing physicality.
But don’t let the slick barrage of one-liners deceive you into thinking there’s no room here for bruising self-examination and perhaps even tentative growth.
“Linda Vista” really is that good.
This new work at Second Stage’s Hayes Theater from Letts is so out of touch with the concerns of the progressive new-play moment as to almost qualify as courageous counter-programming.
Although it sags a bit in places, it coheres in the end, and Barford and Letts give Wheeler precisely the right amount of rot.
Linda Vista doesn’t let anyone off the hook that easily, and if there’s hope to be had, it won’t come cheap.
"Linda Vista" turns out to be an engaging, if flawed, portrait of a modern day everyman who's incredibly smart on the one hand while behaving so inexplicably dumb on the other.
Your ability to get past that question is a gauge of how much you will appreciate this showcase for some impressive acting and very funny writing.
After letting the character loose with his stand-up routine in the first act, the playwright turns Wheeler into a horny bore in the second act.
He’s a heterosexual disaster zone, and one which the playwright (and by extension us) end up feeling a little too ambivalent about.
As central characters go, Wheeler is, admittedly, supremely unlikable.
Like 'Groundhog Day' for the neurotically maladjusted.
'Linda Vista' Has an Ugly View of the Pursuit of Happiness
Ian Barford seizes the role of Wheeler for the kind of tour-de-force performance people talk about long after the curtain has fallen.
Barford, uninhibited and honest, is perfectly cast and leads a uniformly very fine ensemble
Letts' razor-sharp skill at dialogue and characterization will keep most of us riveted

Indeed, your ability to get past that question – and, more generally, your willingness to entertain yet another middle-aged white guy comedy – is a gauge of how much you will appreciate this showcase for some impressive acting and very funny writing.
I enjoyed its locker-room talk; its acerbic humor; its steamily raw sexuality

As written with dynamic energy and force by the expertly aligned Tracy Letts, Wheeler is one of the more difficult people to want to spend time with, let alone more than two hours. Somehow though, much to our surprise, this dark comedy finds its way to respecting itself.
The play delineates a case of toxic masculinity and will most likely fascinate men and infuriate women.

But, as embraced by director Dexter Bullard, it plays like one of those formulaic, comfortably predictable sitcoms that you might have enjoyed twenty years ago, but watching it now makes you cringe at what you once found funny.
No surprise then, that it's dramatically DOA.

A dismal commentary on marriage, relationships and the alpha male. All this would probably be easily acceptable ten years ago, but in the current socio-political ideology it is difficult to subject an audience to this counterculture even though existing remnants are still being unearthed.
